name: Felix Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm carpentry foreman on a new hospital wing, six floors, for one of the big contractors. My crew of twelve does the interior: metal stud walls, plasterboard, ceilings, door frames, all the boxing around the pipes and cables. I'm in at seven, toolbox talk at quarter past, then I'm walking floors with the services engineers fighting over who gets which bit of ceiling space. Hospitals are mad for that, there's oxygen pipes and data cables and everything has to be fire-stopped.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the organising, honestly, getting twelve people and three trades to finish a floor on the same Friday. What wears me out is the changes, a doctor decides a room should be an office instead of a store and I've got to rip out a wall we built last week. I use one of the AI apps now and then to tidy up my daily reports, mostly because my spelling is terrible. Thursday nights I play five-a-side, that keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: First one, then. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, that's what I expected. Something useful for paperwork and not much else. I'm not a big poster online, maybe a comment in the foremen's group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think good, my plan still works. Ana and I have got the house, a small rental flat we bought eight years ago, and a decent pot in the bank. If nothing radical changes, I stay on the bigger jobs till my fifties and step back a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep the crew, keep using the app for reports, keep the flat rented. I'd maybe put a bit more into Diego's college fund, he's fifteen and wants to do engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady as she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan, in numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rental pays most of its own mortgage, and that's done in nine years. Our house is done in fourteen. If I'm still earning a foreman's wage until then, we're in good shape, and Ana's salon covers the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, what would still bother you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Design changes, like I said, and the pace on hospital jobs. There's always a penalty clause if you're late. That's about the contract, not about computers.

S0.say: He'd say it's what he expected: useful for paperwork and not much else. He might leave a comment in the foremen's group chat but wouldn't post more widely.
S0.think: Privately he'd be pleased his long-term plan still holds. He has a house, a rental flat and solid savings, and expects to stay on big jobs until his fifties.
S0.do: Carries on with his crew and keeps using an AI app for daily reports. Keeps the rental flat let and adds a little more to his son's college fund.
S0.quote: The rental pays most of its own mortgage, and that's done in nine years.
S0.fieldNote: Felix thinks in numbers and plans, and his finances are well arranged. He's practical and unexcited about AI, using it only for spelling. His frustrations are about contracts and design changes, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change some things and we'll adjust, same as always. At the foremen's meeting I'd ask the company what they're planning, because I don't want to hear it last. I'd keep it practical, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my part of the job's fairly safe for a while. Coordinating twelve people and three trades in a hospital is messy. What I'd watch is the factory-built wall panels, because if they come in, my crew could drop from twelve to eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools the other foremen are getting good results with, then I'd ask the company to train me on the planning software they pick. If the factory panels come in, I'd volunteer to run the first job that uses them, because it's better to be the foreman they know can do it. Money-wise, no change, maybe a bit more into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little alert, like when the weather turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the crew dropped to eight, who would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who turn up and learn. That's not nice to say, but that's the honest answer. I'd make sure the four leaving got a good reference and a phone number, there's plenty of work around town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. What would convince you a tool works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two foremen I trust say it saved them a day a week, I'm in. One person's not enough, everyone has a favourite gadget. Two is a pattern.

S1.say: He'd say things will change and people will adjust, same as always. At the foremen's meeting he'd ask the company directly what's planned so he doesn't hear it last.
S1.think: Privately he thinks coordinating trades in a hospital stays safe for a while. He watches for factory-built wall panels, which could shrink his crew from twelve to eight.
S1.do: Waits until two trusted foremen report good results, then asks to be trained on the chosen planning software. Volunteers to run the first factory-panel job and adds a little to savings.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little alert, like when the weather turns.
S1.quote: One person's not enough, everyone has a favourite gadget. Two is a pattern.
S1.fieldNote: A textbook steady adopter with a clear rule for when he'll change. He positions himself early on the panel jobs to stay valuable, which is shrewd without being risky. He's frank and unsentimental about who he'd keep on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows what's coming, and anyone who says they do is selling something. I'd say we need a plan from the government and the companies, both, quickly. I wouldn't go to protests, but I'd want answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast for my plan. If robots do partitions and ceilings, the hospital job finishes and the next job might not need a foreman with twelve people, it might need a technician with two machines. And if nobody's working, who rents my flat?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the rental flat in the first few months, while prices hold, and use it to clear most of our house mortgage. That's the big move. I'd cut back on the holiday and the new van, and put Ana's salon income into savings while it lasts. Then I'd see which jobs the robot companies need people for, once I'd heard from someone who'd done one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing spreadsheets at midnight, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the flat so fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everyone loses work in two years, house prices drop and rents go unpaid. I'd rather have a smaller mortgage and no tenant than a big mortgage and a tenant who can't pay. It's simple numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Diego, who wants to be an engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep going, but that the plan might change in the middle. He'd ask if engineers will still exist. I'd tell him I don't know, which he'd hate, he likes answers like me.

S2.say: He'd say nobody really knows what's coming and anyone who claims to is selling something. He'd want a quick plan from government and companies, though he wouldn't join protests.
S2.think: Privately he sees two years as too fast for his financial plan. Robots could replace his crew, and without jobs nobody would rent his flat.
S2.do: Sells the rental flat within months while prices hold and uses the money to clear most of the family mortgage. Cuts the holiday and new van, saves his wife's salon income, and looks into robot company jobs after hearing from someone who has done one.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing spreadsheets at midnight but with a plan.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a smaller mortgage and no tenant than a big mortgage and a tenant who can't pay.
S2.fieldNote: His instinct is to restructure his money rather than his skills. He reasons about the wider economy through his own rental flat, which is a sharp and concrete link. Strong assets and a plan keep him at anxious rather than alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get organised if people stop arguing and start planning. At the foremen's meeting I'd push for a training plan for the crews. Nothing dramatic, just practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Five years puts me at forty-eight with Diego at uni and Lucia finishing school. I'd have time to see which way it goes and move once the path is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first year, I'd keep working and save hard, and keep the flat for now. Around year two or three, once a couple of foremen had moved into running robot install crews, I'd ask to be trained for that. I'd probably sell the flat around year three, before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a long job with a tight deadline, but one you can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm selling up fast to protect the house. With five I can time it, wait for others to show me what works, and sell the flat at a better price. Time lets me do it my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, my best boarder. He's fifty-five, fantastic hands, but he won't touch a phone. Five years gets him to sixty, maybe that's enough. I'd want him out on a good note.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get organised if people plan instead of argue. At the foremen's meeting he'd push for a practical training plan for crews.
S3.think: Privately he thinks he'd be fine, reaching forty-eight with his son at university. He'd have time to see the direction and move once the path is clear.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving in the first year and holds on to the flat for now. Asks for training to run robot install crews around year two or three once others have, and sells the flat about year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a long job with a tight but plannable deadline.
S3.quote: Time lets me do it my way.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time lets him be the steady adopter he is, moving once others have shown the way. His money moves become timed rather than rushed. He shows quiet care for an older colleague nearing retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so let's not panic. I'd want the company to give us a clear plan and training. Maybe I'd say a bit more in the group chat, but sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years almost fits my plan perfectly. Rental flat paid off, house nearly done, kids through school, me at fifty-three. I'd still want to work, but I wouldn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for five or six years as foreman and keep the flat. Around year six, if it's clear, I'd retrain into robot site coordination once others had shown it works. Otherwise I'd be ready to step back early and maybe help Ana in the salon with the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I'd be keeping an eye on it, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd sell the flat fast. Why keep it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, it pays itself off first. The worry was being stuck with a mortgage on it when nobody can pay rent. With ten years, there's no mortgage left to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the day it arrives look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a normal Thursday. Five-a-side in the evening, Diego home from wherever he's working. I'd be fifty-three and I'd have a paid-off flat and a plan. I think I'd sleep fine.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and there's no need to panic. He'd want the company to give clear plans and training, and might post a few sensible comments.
S4.think: Privately he sees ten years fitting his financial plan almost perfectly. By fifty-three the flat would be paid off, the house nearly done and the kids through school.
S4.do: Keeps working as foreman and keeps the rental flat for five or six years. Retrains into robot site coordination around year six if others show it works, or steps back early to help with the salon's books.
S4.feel: Calm, while keeping an eye on things.
S4.quote: With ten years, there's no mortgage left to worry about.
S4.fieldNote: For Felix the decade lines up with his debt schedule, which is why he's calm. He changes his flat decision with clear logic when the contradiction is raised. His picture of the day AGI arrives is completely ordinary, which says a lot about his temperament.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it breaks the plan before the numbers work out. What would help is a clear plan from the company about which jobs they'll still need, and training for those, paid, before the change, not after. And some stability in house prices, but nobody can promise that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the money side, not just the job. Lots of tradespeople my age own a flat or two. If AI hits rents, it hits more than our wages.

headlineQuote: If AI hits rents, it hits more than our wages.
portrait: Felix Alvarez is a 43-year-old carpentry foreman on a new hospital wing, married to a salon owner, with a son of fifteen and a daughter of eleven, plus a rental flat. He uses AI now and then for reports and adopts new tools only after two trusted foremen vouch for them. He's calm through the plateau and steady change, anxious under AGI in two years, when he'd sell the flat to clear the mortgage, and increasingly calm as the warning grows. He thinks about every scenario through his debt schedule, and the decade fits it almost perfectly.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it breaks his financial plan before the numbers work out.
whatWouldHelp: A clear company plan on which jobs will remain, with paid training before the change, and some stability in house prices.
